issues.item: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: The profile is not coherent with a toxic chemical exposure trauma. The selected Threat items are dominated by interpersonal/being-followed danger themes ('someone is following me', lock checking) rather than contamination, health deterioration, environmental exposure, or bodily harm themes that would fit chemical exposure.

issues.item: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: The Maladaptive Strategy item 'Never Alone' is also strongly interpersonal/assault-focused and is hard to reconcile with toxic chemical exposure. 'Avoid Conflict' similarly targets confrontation rather than exposure-related danger, and is not plausibly linked to the selected Threat items or trauma type.

issues.item: Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person
issues.explanation: For toxic chemical exposure, 'Never Alone with another person' is hard to reconcile clinically: it implies fear of interpersonal danger rather than contamination, bodily harm, or environmental exposure. No Trigger, Memory, or Appraisal items support an interpersonal-assault formulation.

issues.item: Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Conflict' also points to interpersonal threat management rather than consequences of chemical exposure. With no corroborating interpersonal threat, appraisal, or memory content, this strategy appears misaligned with the trauma type and the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
issues.explanation: For toxic chemical exposure, avoiding conflict is not a plausible trauma-linked maladaptive strategy unless supported by appraisals about blame, authority, or interpersonal danger, which are absent here. It appears clinically disconnected from the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building
issues.explanation: Avoiding being alone is hard to reconcile with the stated threat pattern. The threat items emphasize generalized unsafety and checking the physical environment, but not collapse, contamination, or medical emergency fears that would make solitude specifically dangerous after chemical exposure.

vignette:
Bao had been an HVAC technician for nearly thirty years, a master of his trade who understood the intricate systems of heating and cooling that kept the city breathing. He was working a commercial job six months ago, a routine replacement of a chiller unit in the sub-basement of an old office building, when a corroded feeder line ruptured. The air filled instantly with the acrid, suffocating bite of refrigerant gas. Disoriented, his lungs burning, he fumbled for the exit only to find the heavy service door had automatically locked behind him. For what felt like an eternity, he was trapped in the chemical fog, pounding on the steel door, his vision blurring as the alarms began to sound far above him. He was found by the fire department, conscious but barely, his body trembling uncontrollably.

The physical effects-the respiratory irritation and dizziness-faded within a week, but a deeper contamination had taken hold. A pervasive sense of threat became Bao's constant companion. His body remained coiled and tense, perpetually ready to react to a danger he couldn't name. At home, he found it impossible to believe his wife, Lien, when she told him he was safe, that the doors were locked and the house was secure. Her words were just sounds, unable to penetrate the certainty of imminent harm that now lived in his bones. This unshakeable conviction that catastrophe was just a moment away began to govern his every action. Relaxing felt like an invitation to disaster; to sit on the sofa after dinner was to lower a shield he couldn't afford to be without, so he would pace the small living room instead. He started avoiding being alone, the silence of an empty room echoing the terrifying isolation of that basement, and would trail Lien from the kitchen to the laundry room, needing her presence as a bulwark against his fear.

His world began to shrink, organized around a single principle: the avoidance of anything that might be stressful. At work, he began turning down jobs that involved basements or confined spaces, citing excuses that grew flimsier with each refusal. His supervisor, once appreciative of his expertise, was growing impatient. At home, the routines that once brought comfort were now sources of obsessive anxiety. Every night, he would check the front door lock not once, but three or four times, pulling on the handle until his knuckles were white, seeking a reassurance that never came. He would circle the house, ensuring every window was latched, his movements rigid and silent. Lien would watch him, her expression a mixture of pity and exhaustion. The man she had married, who was once so steady and calm, had been replaced by a sentinel guarding against an invisible enemy.

The breaking point arrived last week. He was assigned a simple diagnostic job in a residential basement. Standing at the top of the wooden stairs, looking down into the dim light, his heart began to hammer against his ribs. The smell of dust and damp concrete was enough to bring the chemical burn back to his throat. He couldn't move. He called his supervisor and told him he was sick, then drove home in a cold sweat. He knew then that this was not something he could manage on his own. Bao came to therapy not with hope, but with the quiet desperation of a man who can no longer bear the weight of his own vigilance. He is terrified of losing his job and pushing his wife away, but what frightens him most is the chilling belief that if he ever truly lets his guard down, he will not survive it.
